target: AG1's claim that AI is good for society overall because it provides convenience, productivity, accessibility, health, and safety benefits
objection: AI can replace or reshape human work in ways that undermine the economic well-being of many people and businesses, AI can encourage overreliance and misinformation that weakens critical thinking, AI can reproduce and exacerbate racism, and AI can create dangerous privacy risks; taken together, these harms may outweigh the claimed benefits.

target: AG2's claim that AI harms are inevitable and society-wide despite safeguards
objection: Bias, misinformation, privacy, and displacement harms are substantially mitigatable through measures such as audits, human oversight, privacy protections, reskilling, and job redesign, so they are not inevitable at the societal level.

target: AG1's assumption that convenience/productivity benefits can be achieved alongside safeguards that fully neutralize harms
objection: Convenience/productivity AI deployments typically require large-scale data processing and automated decision-making, and those same technical pipelines still leave non-negligible privacy and discrimination harms even when audits, oversight, and policy controls are used.

target: AG2's claim that harms are unavoidable consequences of AI
objection: The harms cited by the opponent—job displacement, misinformation, biased outcomes, and privacy/surveillance risks—depend on how AI is deployed and on data/accountability choices, rather than being unavoidable consequences of AI in general.

target: AG2's overall net-harm conclusion
objection: AI can generate welfare gains in health, safety, accessibility, and productivity, and overall value depends on whether harms fully cancel those gains; there is no evidence that they do so at the society level.

target: AG1's claim that society-wide gains remain net positive
objection: The harms to employment, critical thinking, racial equity, and privacy impose substantial welfare losses and directly offset the same welfare dimensions that AG1 counts as benefits, making net societal welfare plausibly zero or negative.

target: AG2's claim that the opponent's harms eliminate the basis for judging AI good overall
objection: Even if AI causes some economic disruption, misinformation, bias, and privacy risks, those harms do not eliminate the core public-welfare gains in health, inclusion, and safety that support judging AI good for society overall.

target: AG1's claims that AI improves health, inclusion, and workplace safety
objection: Privacy/surveillance harms can worsen health outcomes through stress, chilling effects, and unequal treatment; discriminatory AI outcomes can reduce real access and participation for marginalized groups; and economic displacement can worsen living standards, undercutting workplace-safety improvements.

target: AG2's claim that harms eliminate the welfare gains
objection: AI can also be used for harm-reduction purposes such as workforce transition support, misinformation detection, bias auditing, and privacy-preserving processing, so it is not established that AI harms must dominate the net social outcome.

target: AG1's assumption that audits, oversight, and privacy protections are available and effective enough to make AI safe
objection: In real-world deployments, biased outcomes, misinformation amplification, and privacy breaches still occur at scale despite such safeguards, showing that these harm-reduction tools are often unavailable or ineffective in society-relevant settings.

target: AG2's claim that productivity gains do not translate into societal benefit
objection: Productivity and learning gains can raise overall output and living standards, offsetting some economic disruption, and AI also improves health, safety, and accessibility, so broad welfare gains can still justify a positive overall judgment.

target: AG1's claim that productivity gains offset economic harms
objection: AI-driven economic disruption can reduce employment and incomes for many people, and productivity/learning gains do not automatically translate into improved economy-wide living standards for those affected by displacement.

target: AG1's claim that AI is not good overall because the opponent's harms are not compelling enough
objection: Most deployed AI systems are complex and proprietary, with limited explanations; critical thinking requires contestable reasons; historical-data AI can reproduce racism; and sensitive-data processing plus limited transparency create privacy risks that individuals cannot meaningfully control.

target: AG2's assumption that transparency, contestability, and privacy harms cannot be mitigated
objection: AI can be deployed with human-understandable explanations, appeal mechanisms, bias monitoring and correction, and privacy-preserving design plus user control, so critical thinking, discrimination, and privacy harms can be substantially mitigated.

target: AG1's assumption that those mitigation mechanisms are reliably available in real deployments
objection: Meaningful protection against critical-thinking erosion, discrimination persistence, and privacy risk requires user-accessible reasons, contestation, and data control, but proprietary models, limited disclosure, and cross-border deployment often prevent those safeguards from being effectively implemented and enforced.

target: AG1's claim that opt-out/consent can secure meaningful control over AI-derived inferences
objection: AI profiling can infer sensitive attributes from data users did not knowingly provide, and even with privacy-preserving processing and opt-out mechanisms, people cannot reliably prevent or control the downstream use of those derived inferences.

target: AG2's claim that profiling and derived inferences inevitably create dangerous privacy risks
objection: Privacy-preserving architectures, data minimization, differential privacy, federated learning, and on-device inference can sharply limit sensitive inferences and dangerous derived profiles, so AI need not create uncontrollable privacy risks.

target: AG1's claim that privacy-preserving deployment can eliminate dangerous privacy risks
objection: Attribute-inference and membership-reconstruction risks can still arise even with aggregation, differential privacy, or federated learning, and many real-world profiling systems expose outputs or queries that enable repeated inference attempts, so privacy-preserving choices cannot reliably prevent those risks.

target: AG2's assumption that privacy governance cannot make AI use societally acceptable
objection: Enforceable governance with disclosure, purpose limits, auditing, and user rights can give people and regulators meaningful control over profiling data and derived inferences, reducing privacy risks from dangerous to manageable levels.

target: AG1's assumption that such governance can be reliably implemented and enforced
objection: Many real-world AI systems are proprietary and black-box, with limited access for audits and regulators, and cross-border deployment often prevents effective enforcement of disclosure, auditing, and user-rights rules.

target: AG2's claim that opt-out cannot prevent harmful downstream use of derived inferences
objection: Consent-aware data lineage and retention can be built into AI systems so that derived inferences are tied to consent status and blocked from downstream reuse when a user opts out.

target: AG1's claim that opt-out/consent can stop downstream reuse of derived inferences
objection: In many profiling systems, derived inferences are reused across caching, logging, other models, and retraining workflows, so user opt-out cannot reliably prevent all downstream use and therefore does not secure meaningful control.

target: AG2's claim that opt-out cannot reliably prevent downstream use in these deployments
objection: Consent-aware retention and lineage can be built so that derived inferences are labeled by consent status and not reused across downstream channels, making opt-out effective in relevant deployments.

target: AG1's claim that consent-aware enforcement solves the privacy problem
objection: Real-world multi-stage AI pipelines are proprietary and cross-system, and derived artifacts are generally not labeled in a way that downstream systems can reliably enforce per-user consent status, so consent-aware retention and lineage are often ineffective.
